title: Principles of Analytical Chemistry
description: Accuracy, precision, calibration, and the analytical process

concepts.title: Accuracy, Precision, and Error
concepts.contentHtml:
Two fundamental concepts that are often confused:

Accuracy: how close a measurement is to the true (accepted) value. Measured by systematic error (bias).
Precision: how reproducible measurements are — how closely repeated measurements agree with each other. Measured by random error (scatter).

A method can be precise but inaccurate (consistently wrong in the same direction — systematic error), accurate but imprecise (results scattered around the true value), or ideally both. Errors are classified as:
— Systematic: consistent bias (faulty calibration, contamination, wrong standard) — can be identified and corrected
— Random: unpredictable scatter from uncontrolled variables — reduced by averaging replicate measurements
— Gross errors: blunders (discarded by statistical tests like Grubbs' test)

concepts.title: Calibration and Standards
concepts.contentHtml:
All quantitative analytical methods require calibration — relating instrument response to known analyte concentrations using standards.

Types of standards:
— External calibration: measure a series of standards at known concentrations, build a calibration curve (response vs concentration), then read off unknown concentrations. Assumes the unknown matrix is the same as the standard matrix.
— Standard addition: add known amounts of analyte directly to the unknown sample. Corrects for matrix effects — different sample components affect the analytical signal. Used when matrix matching is difficult (e.g., trace metals in seawater).
— Internal standard: add a fixed amount of a different compound (similar properties, doesn't appear in sample) to all samples and standards. Corrects for variable extraction efficiency and instrument drift.

concepts.title: Detection Limits and Figures of Merit
concepts.contentHtml:
Key performance characteristics of any analytical method:

— Limit of detection (LOD): the lowest concentration distinguishable from a blank with statistical confidence. Typically defined as signal_blank + 3σ_blank, where σ is the standard deviation of blank measurements.
— Limit of quantitation (LOQ): signal_blank + 10σ_blank — lowest concentration that can be measured with acceptable precision and accuracy.
— Linear dynamic range: the concentration range over which response is linear.
— Selectivity (specificity): ability to measure the analyte without interference from other species.
— Sensitivity: the slope of the calibration curve (Δsignal / Δconcentration) — how small a change in concentration produces a detectable signal change.

Regulatory methods (EPA, FDA, pharmacopoeias) require formal method validation against all these criteria.

title: Titrimetry
description: Acid-base, redox, complexometric, and precipitation titrations

concepts.title: Acid–Base Titrations
concepts.contentHtml:
A titration adds a reagent of known concentration (titrant) to the analyte solution until the reaction is complete. The equivalence point is where stoichiometric amounts have reacted; the endpoint is where the indicator changes — ideally these coincide.

For a strong acid–strong base titration (HCl + NaOH), the equivalence point is pH 7. The titration curve has a steep S-shape around the equivalence point.

For a weak acid–strong base titration (e.g., acetic acid + NaOH): equivalence point is above pH 7 (the conjugate base hydrolyses). The half-equivalence point is where pH = pKa of the weak acid — very useful for determining pKa values experimentally.

Indicator choice matters: the indicator's pKin should be within the steep portion of the curve. Phenolphthalein (pH 8.2–10) suits weak acid/strong base; methyl orange (pH 3.1–4.4) suits strong acid/weak base.

concepts.title: Redox and Complexometric Titrations
concepts.contentHtml:
Redox titrations exploit electron transfer reactions. The permanganate titration is classic: KMnO₄ (deep purple) oxidises Fe²⁺ in acid solution; the endpoint is the first permanent faint pink colour as excess MnO₄⁻ remains unreduced. Permanganate is its own indicator.

Other common redox titrations: iodometric titrations (I₂/thiosulfate), cerimetric (Ce⁴⁺ as oxidant), and dichromate titrations for alcohol in breathalysers.

Complexometric titrations use a chelating agent — usually EDTA⁴⁻ — to bind metal ions. EDTA forms stable 1:1 complexes with virtually all metal ions regardless of charge. The endpoint is detected with a metallochromic indicator (e.g., Eriochrome Black T, EBT), which changes colour when EDTA displaces the indicator from the metal–indicator complex. Used to measure water hardness (Ca²⁺ + Mg²⁺) and many metals.

concepts.title: Titration Calculations
concepts.contentHtml:
The fundamental titration equation links moles at the equivalence point:

n_analyte = n_titrant (adjusted for stoichiometry)

or equivalently: C₁V₁ = C₂V₂ (for 1:1 reactions)

For non-1:1 stoichiometry, adjust: n₁/z₁ = n₂/z₂ (equivalents).

Back titration: add excess titrant, then titrate the excess with a second titrant. Used when the direct reaction is slow or the analyte decomposes (e.g., determining calcium by adding excess EDTA then back-titrating unreacted EDTA with Zn²⁺).

Standardisation: titrant concentrations are determined precisely by titrating against a primary standard — a pure, stable, high-molar-mass compound (e.g., potassium hydrogen phthalate for NaOH; sodium oxalate for KMnO₄; potassium dichromate for thiosulfate).

title: Chromatography
description: Separation principles, HPLC, GC, and TLC

concepts.title: Principles of Chromatographic Separation
concepts.contentHtml:
Chromatography separates mixtures by partitioning components between a stationary phase and a mobile phase. Components that interact more strongly with the stationary phase move more slowly; those with more affinity for the mobile phase move faster — and the mixture separates.

Key performance terms:
— Retention time (t_R): time for a compound to travel through the column under set conditions
— Resolution (R_s): how well two adjacent peaks are separated. R_s ≥ 1.5 is baseline resolution.
— Theoretical plates (N): a measure of column efficiency. More plates = sharper, narrower peaks
— Selectivity (α): ratio of retention factors of two compounds — reflects the chemical basis of separation

The van Deemter equation describes how flow rate affects peak broadening: H = A + B/u + Cu, where H is plate height and u is linear velocity. There is an optimal flow rate that minimises H (maximises N).

concepts.title: HPLC and Gas Chromatography
concepts.contentHtml:
High-Performance Liquid Chromatography (HPLC): a pump drives the liquid mobile phase through a column packed with fine particles (typically 3–5 μm silica-based stationary phase). High pressure is needed because of small particle size.

Modes: reverse-phase HPLC is most common — non-polar stationary phase (C18 bonded silica), polar mobile phase (water/acetonitrile/methanol). Non-polar compounds elute last. Used for drugs, biomolecules, environmental contaminants.

Gas Chromatography (GC): volatile compounds are carried by an inert gas (He, N₂) through a long capillary column coated with a liquid stationary phase. Temperature programming separates compounds by boiling point and polarity. GC is coupled to mass spectrometry (GC-MS) for identification — the gold standard for volatile organics (drugs of abuse, flavour compounds, blood-alcohol).

concepts.title: Thin-Layer and Ion-Exchange Chromatography
concepts.contentHtml:
Thin-layer chromatography (TLC): a silica or alumina layer on a plate; spots of sample are applied and the plate developed in solvent. The Rf value = distance travelled by spot / distance travelled by solvent front. TLC is fast, cheap, and widely used in organic labs to monitor reactions and check purity.

Ion-exchange chromatography (IEC): stationary phase carries fixed charges that attract oppositely charged analytes. Cation exchangers (negatively charged, e.g., –SO₃⁻) retain cations; anion exchangers retain anions. Elution is achieved by increasing salt concentration or changing pH. Used to separate amino acids (classic ninhydrin amino acid analyser), proteins, and nucleotides.

Size-exclusion chromatography (SEC/GPC): separates by molecular size — large molecules cannot enter pores, elute first; small molecules enter pores and elute last. Used to determine molecular weight of polymers and proteins.
mathExpressions: R_f = \frac{\text{distance moved by solute}}{\text{distance moved by solvent front}}

title: Spectroscopic Analysis
description: Atomic absorption, emission spectroscopy, and mass spectrometry

concepts.title: Atomic Spectroscopy
concepts.contentHtml:
Atomic spectroscopy determines which elements are present and at what concentration by measuring light emitted or absorbed by atoms.

Flame atomic absorption spectrometry (FAAS): sample is aspirated into a flame (typically air–acetylene), atomised, and a hollow-cathode lamp shines light of a characteristic wavelength through the flame. Atoms absorb the specific wavelength. Absorbance ∝ concentration (Beer–Lambert law). FAAS is simple, robust, and element-specific but analyses one element at a time.

Inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectrometry (ICP-OES): sample is injected into an argon plasma (~6,000–10,000 K). Excited atoms emit light at characteristic wavelengths, detected simultaneously for many elements. Superior detection limits (~ppb) and multi-element capability. Used for environmental, geological, and food samples.

concepts.title: Mass Spectrometry
concepts.contentHtml:
Mass spectrometry (MS) measures the mass-to-charge ratio (m/z) of ions, giving precise molecular masses and fragmentation patterns.

Stages:
1. Ionisation: create gas-phase ions. Electron ionisation (EI) — harsh, gives fragmentation (good for identification). Electrospray ionisation (ESI) — gentle, preserves large molecules (proteins, nucleic acids). MALDI — for large biomolecules.
2. Mass analyser: separates ions by m/z. Time-of-flight (TOF), quadrupole, orbitrap (ultra-high resolution).
3. Detection: ion current detected and recorded as a mass spectrum.

Applications: GC-MS for volatile organics; LC-MS/MS for drugs and metabolites; HRMS for exact molecular formula determination; proteomics (bottom-up MS of peptides from protein digestion).

concepts.title: Electroanalytical Methods
concepts.contentHtml:
Electroanalytical chemistry uses electrode reactions to measure analyte concentration.

Potentiometry: measures cell potential at zero (or negligible) current. The glass pH electrode is the archetypal example — potential depends on [H⁺] via the Nernst equation. Ion-selective electrodes (ISEs) measure specific ions: F⁻, Na⁺, K⁺, Ca²⁺, NO₃⁻. Used in clinical chemistry (blood electrolytes) and in-field water quality monitoring.

Voltammetry: measures current as potential is scanned. Cyclic voltammetry (CV) probes electrochemical behaviour of redox species and is used to study enzyme active sites, drug redox chemistry, and battery materials. Stripping voltammetry achieves parts-per-trillion detection limits for trace metals (preconcentrate by electrodeposition, then strip).

title: Advanced Techniques and Real-World Applications
description: Hyphenated methods, environmental analysis, and forensic chemistry

concepts.title: Hyphenated Techniques
concepts.contentHtml:
Hyphenated techniques couple a separation method with a spectroscopic detector, gaining both the resolving power of chromatography and the identification power of spectroscopy.

Key hyphenated techniques:
— GC-MS: gold standard for volatile organics — retention time (GC) + mass spectrum (MS). The NIST mass spectral library contains >350,000 spectra for matching.
— LC-MS/MS: non-volatile and thermally labile compounds (drugs, metabolites, peptides). Triple quadrupole MS/MS (MRM mode) gives sub-ppb quantitation and superb selectivity.
— ICP-MS: separation not needed for elemental analysis; plasma ionises everything, quadrupole or TOF separates isotopes. Ultra-trace metals to sub-ppt in environmental and geological samples.
— LC-NMR: structural characterisation directly from chromatographic fractions — powerful but slow.

concepts.title: Environmental and Clinical Analysis
concepts.contentHtml:
Analytical chemistry underpins environmental monitoring, food safety, and clinical diagnostics.

Environmental: EPA methods specify exactly how to measure pollutants. Priority pollutants (PAHs, PCBs, dioxins) measured by GC-MS. Heavy metals (Pb, Hg, Cd, As) by ICP-MS. Nutrient ions (NO₃⁻, PO₄³⁻) by ion chromatography (IC). Pesticides in food by QuEChERS extraction + LC-MS/MS.

Clinical chemistry: blood glucose by glucose oxidase biosensor (electrochemical). Electrolytes (Na⁺, K⁺, Cl⁻, HCO₃⁻) by ISEs. Drugs of abuse in urine by immunoassay screening, confirmed by GC-MS or LC-MS/MS. Hemoglobin A1c (diabetes marker) by HPLC. Newborn screening for 50+ metabolic disorders by tandem MS (LC-MS/MS of dried blood spots).

concepts.title: Forensic Chemistry and Method Validation
concepts.contentHtml:
Forensic chemistry applies analytical techniques to legal questions. Chain of custody ensures sample integrity. Key analyses:
— Illicit drugs: colour spot tests (Marquis, Scott) for presumptive ID; GC-MS or LC-MS/MS for confirmation
— Firearms residue: SEM-EDX identifies gunshot residue particles containing Pb, Sb, Ba
— Document analysis: ink dating by TLC or HPLC
— Toxicology: blood alcohol by headspace GC; postmortem drug screening by LC-MS/MS

Method validation is required before any regulated analytical method is used. Validation parameters: accuracy (% recovery), precision (repeatability/reproducibility), linearity, range, LOD/LOQ, specificity, robustness. FDA 21 CFR Part 11 and ICH Q2 guidelines govern pharmaceutical validation. A validated method means the result can be trusted — and defended in court.

title: Mass Spectrometry in Depth
description: Weighing molecules one ion at a time

concepts.title: Ionization Methods
concepts.contentHtml:
Mass spectrometry needs ions. The ionization method shapes what molecules are amenable.

• Electron ionization (EI): vaporized analyte hit by 70 eV electrons; fragments extensively. Used for small volatile organics with library matching.
• Electrospray ionization (ESI): spraying solution into a charged mist generates ions softly. Workhorse for proteins, drugs, polar metabolites.
• MALDI: matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization for peptides, proteins, oligosaccharides — laser blasts a co-crystallized matrix to release ions.

Soft ionization preserves the parent molecule; hard ionization fragments it. Choose accordingly.

concepts.title: Mass Analyzers
concepts.contentHtml:
Several physics, all sorting ions by m/z:

• Quadrupole: simple, robust, modest resolution.
• Time-of-flight (TOF): ions accelerated to common kinetic energy; lighter ones arrive first.
• Ion trap (Orbitrap, FT-ICR): trap ions in fields and measure their oscillation frequencies. Highest resolution; routine ppm-level mass accuracy.

Tandem MS (MS/MS) selects a precursor ion, fragments it, measures fragments — gives structural information beyond mass alone.

concepts.title: Proteomics & Metabolomics
concepts.contentHtml:
LC-MS/MS underpins proteomics — identification and quantification of thousands of proteins in a single experiment. Bottom-up: digest proteins to peptides, separate by LC, identify by MS/MS, infer protein composition.

Metabolomics profiles small-molecule metabolites comprehensively. Untargeted MS detects thousands of features; targeted assays quantify specific metabolites with high precision.

Both fields rely on mass accuracy, software for spectrum interpretation, and reference databases. They've transformed clinical diagnostics, drug development, and systems biology.

concepts.title: Why Imaging Matters
concepts.contentHtml:
Bulk analysis tells you what's there. Imaging tells you where. The same total amount of a molecule might be uniformly distributed (likely benign) or concentrated in one organelle (potentially crucial).

Modern analytical microscopy combines spatial resolution with chemical specificity — a major frontier of analytical chemistry.

concepts.title: Fluorescence and Super-Resolution
concepts.contentHtml:
Fluorescence microscopy uses dyes (or fluorescent proteins) to label specific molecules. Conventional resolution is limited to ~λ/2 (~250 nm) by Abbe's diffraction limit.

Super-resolution techniques (STED, PALM, STORM) shatter this limit by various tricks. Spatial resolution down to 20 nm is now routine. Hell, Betzig, and Moerner shared the 2014 Nobel.

Imaging single molecules, tracking individual proteins in live cells, watching DNA replication — all newly possible.

concepts.title: Mass Spec Imaging
concepts.contentHtml:
MALDI imaging raster-scans a tissue section with a laser, producing a mass spectrum at every pixel. Map drug distributions, lipid heterogeneity, biomarkers in tissue — without prior labeling.

Spatial resolutions of 10-50 µm are now common; advanced techniques reach single cells.

Combined with cryo-EM, atomic force microscopy, electron tomography, and atom probe tomography for materials, modern analytical imaging spans atomic to organismal scales.

title: Sensors, Wearables & On-Site Analysis
description: Bringing the lab to the sample

concepts.title: Electrochemical Biosensors
concepts.contentHtml:
The glucose meter is the textbook biosensor: an enzyme (glucose oxidase) embedded on an electrode generates current proportional to glucose concentration. Cheap, robust, fast.

Continuous glucose monitors now sample subcutaneously every few minutes, transmitting data wirelessly. Diabetes management has been transformed.

Other biosensors detect lactate, glutamate, neurotransmitters, environmental contaminants — same principles, different recognition elements.

concepts.title: Lateral Flow & Point-of-Care
concepts.contentHtml:
The familiar pregnancy test, COVID rapid antigen test, and dozens of others use lateral flow immunoassays: liquid wicks across a strip, picks up gold nanoparticle-labeled antibodies, accumulates at a test line if the analyte is present.

Robust, cheap, no power needed, results in minutes. Hundreds of millions of LFA tests deployed during COVID — a triumph of low-tech analytical chemistry at scale.

concepts.title: Wearable Chemistry
concepts.contentHtml:
Wearable sensors monitor sweat composition (electrolytes, glucose, cortisol), interstitial fluid, breath, and skin temperature. Some are commercial; many remain research devices.

Combining microfluidics, flexible electronics, and electrochemical sensing on adhesive patches, wearables aim for continuous health monitoring outside clinical settings.

The future may include drug-monitoring patches that detect non-adherence, inflammation markers as early disease signals, and dehydration sensors for athletes — analytical chemistry on the body.
